docs.title: A Course for Language Technology Consultants
docs.text: In production — this course is being built through the repo's 8-stage production pipeline, tracked on issue #40. The design document (00-design.md) was approved, and all content — lessons 01–08, the scenario bank, the mentor guide, and the quiz — is fully drafted, has passed alignment review (Stage 4) and SME fact-check (Stage 5). Its current stage is tracked on the board. Run /next-step supporting-pre-publishing-checks to see where it stands.

docs.title: About This Course
docs.text:
Audience: Language Technology Consultants who support translation teams — not the translators themselves. You are the person a team calls when the pre-publishing checks are producing results nobody can interpret, or when the typesetter has sent the files back.

Goal: Lead a translation team through the pre-publishing text checks in Paratext, from a consultant-checked draft to publication-ready output the typesetter can accept, and advise the team on the decisions the checks surface.

Scope: The text checks — comparing parallel passages, proper names and biblical terms, numbers/weights/measures, the final formatting-check pass with its draft-print verification, and the glossary-linking operation and its checks (over-linking vs. first-per-section). The publication furniture — illustrations, front and back matter, and glossary content itself (as opposed to the linking operation) — is a separate course, not yet built.

Outcome level: 3 - Independent — you run the pass unaided and advise the team. That claim is earned through a mandatory, mentor-reviewed scenario bank, not a self-check rubric: a mentor scores your reasoning on each scenario against the mentor guide's watch-for list, since independence at this level is demonstrated through coaching quality, not a single correct answer.

docs.title: Relationship to the team workbook
docs.text:
This course is the consultant-facing counterpart to Scripture Pre-publishing Checks — the multi-chapter workbook ("Finalizing Your Translation for Publication") that a team works through during the final pre-publishing workshop. That workbook is written for experienced translators doing the work; this course prepares the consultant who supports them.

Use them together: the workbook is the handout you give the team; this course is your own preparation. Both follow Stage 6 of the Paratext Training Manual.

docs.title: Lesson 1: Supporting the Final Turn
docs.text:
Estimated time: 25 minutes

Purpose: Before you study any single check, see where your work fits in the whole translation process. You will learn why checks that were "already done" must be run again. You will also learn what your job is, and what it is not, when you support a team.

Watch the video: To be recorded at stage 8.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
You will be able to:

  • Describe the translation process as a 6-stage spiral.
  • Explain why Stage 6 (pre-publishing) is the "final turn", when earlier checks are run again until there are zero errors.
  • State your role in a pre-publishing check session: diagnose, coach, and never touch the keyboard.
  • Decide whether an issue is yours to resolve, the team's translation decision, or something to escalate.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Think of a time a team said "we already did that check". Later, that check still had problems. What happened? Did anyone go back and look closely? Or did the team trust the earlier pass and move on?

Keep that memory in mind. This course comes back to this pattern again and again.

docs.title: The 6-stage spiral
docs.text:
A Bible translation project moves through six stages before publication. Think of it as a spiral, not a straight line. Comparison, terms, formatting and other checks come back more than once, each time at a higher level of polish.

These checks do not run on a fixed schedule at every stage. Some get attention early and again later. Others are missed at one stage and only show up at another.

The key fact: errors can be introduced, or first appear, at any stage. So a real final check cannot assume that earlier stages caught everything.

docs.title: Stage 6: the final turn
docs.text:
Stage 6 is pre-publishing. It is the final turn of the spiral. Anything missed, introduced or left unresolved earlier is still in the text. The typesetter and reviewers will treat this pass as final. So the team runs the earlier checks again. This time they drive them to zero errors.

Long, high-volume checks still find errors at Stage 6, even when the team "already did" them. The wordlist is the main example. It covers tens of thousands of words, and no single earlier pass catches everything.

docs.title: Start with the Project Plan
docs.text:
You already know Paratext's Project Plan from earlier training. It is the "Assignments and Progress" view: a checklist of required tasks for each stage. Each task shows a live status, such as "3 issues" or "No issues".

At Stage 6, start here. You do not need to rebuild the status by hand. The Project Plan re-runs the basic checks automatically and keeps the status current. You can also rerun any single check directly from there.

docs.title: "No issues" can be false-clean
docs.text:
A "No issues" status only shows what the checks can see. Two user overrides can hide errors:

  • denied errors;
  • a blanket-approved status, such as a wordlist where every word is marked Correct.

An automatic recheck does not undo either override. So the Project Plan can look clean while errors sit underneath.

This is a false-clean result: an "all clear" that nobody earned. It can also come from a check that was skipped. It is the spine of this course: the one idea that runs through every lesson. Errors get missed or waved through when a team is sure a check is "already done". So "we already did that" is the trap.

Each check-area lesson shows what false-clean looks like in that tool. For now, learn the pattern: sometimes you must look at the actual results, not only the summary status.

docs.title: Your role: diagnose and coach
docs.text:
At Stage 6, your job is not to fix the team's text. You do not speak their language. Your job is to:

  1. Diagnose the cause of what a check finds, not just the symptom.
  2. Explain it in plain words that the team can act on.
  3. Coach them through the fix. The translator makes every correction, at their own keyboard. The team's own workbook teaches the same rule.

docs.title: Yours, the team's, or escalate
docs.text:
Not everything you find is yours to resolve. Not everything is the team's decision either. Sort each issue into one of three groups:

  • Yours: a tool or process problem that you can diagnose and coach the team through. Examples: a status set wrongly, a check result the team misunderstood, or glossary links at the wrong scope (over-linked).
  • The team's: a real translation decision. Examples: how a parallel passage should read, or what a rendering should be. You confirm the check ran and the team reviewed it. You do not judge the language content.
  • Escalate: a tool problem you cannot diagnose goes to an LT mentor. A content or translation question that needs a trained eye on Scripture goes to a Translation Consultant.

Key takeaways

  • Errors can appear at any stage, so Stage 6 re-runs earlier checks to zero errors.
  • Start with the Project Plan, but watch for a false-clean result underneath it.
  • You diagnose and coach. The translator makes every correction.
  • Sort every issue: yours, the team's, or escalate.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
✏️ Try this: Four short exercises. Try each one without looking back. Then check your answers against the Content section above.

  1. Sort these issues. For each one, write "yours", "the team's" or "escalate". If you escalate, name who you go to.
  2. A check status was set wrongly.
  3. The team is not sure how a parallel passage should read.
  4. Glossary links were applied to every occurrence instead of the right scope.
  5. A tool problem that you cannot diagnose.
  6. A content question that needs a trained eye on Scripture.
  7. Explain what "No issues" does not tell you. Write two sentences. In the first, say what the checks have really confirmed. In the second, say what an automatic recheck does not undo. Name both user overrides.
  8. Find it in the Project Plan. Open the Project Plan (the "Assignments and Progress" view) in a project you support. Pick one task and read its status. Then find where you would rerun that one check. You only need to find both things. You are not reviewing the project.
  9. Ask "how", not "whether". Write one question for a team. It should ask how a check status became clear, not whether it is clear. Then write one sentence on why this is the better question. Use the idea of a false-clean result.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Think of one team you support now, or will support in future. Where are they most likely to say "we already did that" about a check that still needs a real look? Name the check area if you can.

Next step: Write down that team and check area. You will use it again in the check-area lessons.

Coming up: Lesson 2 uses this "confirm, don't trust" habit on the wordlist and Biblical Terms. In this check area, blanket approval is a real, documented field problem. After that, the course continues:

  • Lesson 3: Parallel Passages, then Lesson 4: Numbers and Measures
  • Lesson 5: Structural Checks, then Lesson 6: Punctuation Before Typesetting
  • Lesson 7: Glossary Linking, then Lesson 8: Layout and the Draft-PDF Read-Through
  • Finally, the scenario bank and the quiz

docs.title: Lesson 2: Wordlist and Biblical Terms
docs.text:
Estimated time: 30 minutes

Purpose: Support a team through two check areas: the wordlist (spelling) and the Biblical Terms tool. Each one can look finished when it is not. You learn to spot this and coach the team to a real fix, without touching their keyboard.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
You will be able to:

  • Recognize that Paratext cannot show whether a wordlist was blanket-approved, and ask the team directly.
  • Coach the team to reset the whole wordlist to Undecided when there is doubt, and review it again together.

You will be able to:

  • Recognize an unfinished Biblical Terms list: blank renderings presented as done, or old and duplicate renderings that were never cleaned up.
  • Coach the team to complete and clean up the Biblical Terms list.
  • Diagnose a Project Biblical Terms list that is too big and slows Send/Receive or performance, and advise the team on right-sizing it.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text: ✏️ Reflection: A project's wordlist can hold tens of thousands of words. Imagine you are the translator, after weeks of drafting. What would tempt you to mark every word "correct" and move on? This is not laziness. It is tiredness. This lesson helps you spot it and handle it with the team.

docs.title: Wordlist: a clean list may not be a checked list
docs.text:
Every word in the wordlist has one of three spelling statuses: Correct, Incorrect or Undecided.

This problem is real. In one field case, a wordlist of thousands of words was blanket-approved. Every word was marked Correct, but nobody really reviewed them. Words can also stay Undecided and never be followed up. That gives the same false picture of a finished list.

WARNING: Paratext has no technical way to detect a blanket-approved wordlist. The tool does not show whether a word was reviewed on its own or approved with many others at once. The Project Plan only shows a count of words marked Incorrect. It does not count Undecided words, and it cannot show bulk approval. So zero Incorrect words in the Project Plan proves nothing.

docs.title: What to do about the wordlist
docs.text:
1. Ask the team directly. Did they review the words one by one, or approve them in bulk?
  2. If there is any doubt, reset the entire wordlist to Undecided. Reset the whole list, not only the words that look suspect. This loses nothing. The words and their spelling data stay the same. Only the approval status resets.
  3. Review the list again with the team. Explain why each flagged word was raised. Pay special attention to words that are split or joined incorrectly. These are common in a mass-approved list.
  4. Let the translator do the work. You explain and coach. The translator reviews and corrects each word.

docs.title: Biblical Terms: blank renderings
docs.text:
Every term in the Biblical Terms tool starts with a gloss and a blank rendering. The gloss is in English, or in the source language of a localized version. The blank rendering is highlighted (for example, in orange). It shows the text "Double click to enter rendering(s) from project text."

This is not a bug. It is the tool's normal starting state. The team's task is simple: work through the list and add a rendering for each term from their own project text.

A term still at its default, unfilled state — not an error, just unfinished.

The risk is that a team presents a partly-done list as "done". This is a false-clean result. Do not just look over the list. Check the Found column on each row, for example "2/2" found, against a row that is still blank.

  • Diagnose: Open the list and check the Found count row by row. Do not trust a general "we did the Biblical Terms".
  • Coach: The team fills in the remaining blank rows themselves, from their own project text.

docs.title: Biblical Terms: old and duplicate renderings
docs.text:
A term can collect several renderings over time. Many of them may no longer be found in the current text. For example, the team adds a correct rendering later, but never deletes the old one. The old one may be wrong. This clutters the list. It becomes hard to tell which rendering the team means to use now.

Renderings pile up over time — the Found column tells you which one is actually live.

  • Diagnose: Look for terms with several renderings. Use the Found count to see which ones are still in the text and which are old leftovers.
  • Coach: The team reviews all the renderings for the term. They confirm which ones are current and correct. By this stage every context has been translated. So a rendering that is not found anywhere in the text is an old leftover. They remove those themselves.

NOTE: A less common pattern is a rendering that is only the first word of the verse, repeated across a term's occurrences. A support.bible programmer says the likely cause is Paratext's Guess Renderings feature. The team probably ran it before the project had enough translated text. With too little data, it can guess the verse's first word as the rendering. This happens automatically, so the translator may not notice it. Do not start your check with this pattern. But if you see it, this is the likely cause.

TIP: To find this pattern quickly, open a term's occurrences. Step through them with the down arrow. You do not need to read each one closely. A rendering that is just the verse's first word stands out when you move through the list quickly.

docs.title: Biblical Terms: project list size
docs.text:
In one field case, a consultant added the entire "All Biblical Terms" list into the Project Biblical Terms list. This is different from selecting a list to view it. Adding puts every term into the project itself.

Paratext's help describes the two lists like this:

  • All Biblical Terms lists every Greek, Hebrew and Aramaic term that occurs 500 times or less in the original text. This can be tens of thousands of entries, depending on the project's scope. The SME has seen a whole-Bible project where this list had about 20,000 entries.
  • Major Biblical Terms is a curated subset of just over 8,500 terms, organized into semantic domains.

So adding the whole "All" list loads tens of thousands of entries, not a few thousand. This makes the project bigger and slows Send/Receive and performance. The slowdown comes from adding the terms to the project list. It does not come from viewing a large list.

It was hard to convince the team of this cause. A non-technical team does not easily connect "we added a big list of terms" with "Send/Receive is now slow". The size of the list is not easy to see from inside the tool.

  • Diagnose: Check whether the Project Biblical Terms list has grown far beyond the terms the project actually uses.
  • Advise: Help the team right-size it. The project list should hold the terms relevant to their translation, not the full reference list.

docs.title: Biblical Terms: several separate lists
docs.text:
The Open Biblical Terms List dialog holds several separate lists. They include:

  • Major Biblical Terms
  • All Biblical Terms
  • NT Key Biblical Terms
  • Inclusive/Exclusive Pronouns
  • Younger/Older Siblings, and others.

Numbers is another separate entry there (see Lesson 4). There is no Measures list. A new combined list for numbers, weights and measures is replacing the older Numbers list. Not every team's Paratext version will have it at the same time. So do not assume that every project's lists look the same, or behave the same way.

Numbers is its own entry here, separate from the other lists.

Key takeaways

  • Paratext cannot detect a blanket-approved wordlist. The Project Plan counts only Incorrect words. Ask the team directly. If there is doubt, reset the whole wordlist to Undecided (this loses nothing) and review it again together.
  • Blank renderings are the normal starting state in Biblical Terms, not a bug. Check the Found column row by row to confirm the list is really complete.
  • Old and duplicate renderings pile up. Coach the team to remove the ones no longer found in the text.
  • Adding a huge list to the Project Biblical Terms slows Send/Receive. Help the team right-size it.
  • You diagnose and coach. The team makes the fixes. You never touch their keyboard.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
✏️ Try this: Four short exercises on this lesson. Try each one without looking back. Then check your answers against the Content section above.

  1. Why zero is not enough. Name the three spelling statuses a word can have. Then write one or two sentences: why does a Project Plan with zero Incorrect words not prove that the team reviewed the wordlist?
  2. Sort two rows. For each row, write what it tells you and what you check to confirm it.
  3. Row A has a highlighted rendering with the text "Double click to enter rendering(s) from project text."
  4. Row B has five renderings on one term. Most of them are no longer found in the text.

Then say which row is the tool's normal starting state, and which shows something that needs cleaning up. 3. Find the column. Open the Biblical Terms list in a project you support. Pick one row. Look at its Found count and its rendering(s). Write which state the row is in: blank default, one current rendering, or several renderings to review. One row is enough. 4. Explain it to the team. A team says, "We only opened the All Biblical Terms list. Why is Send/Receive slow?" Write two or three sentences you could say to them. Explain the difference between selecting a list to view it and adding it to the project. Use the list sizes from this lesson.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Which check area is more likely to come up with a team you support now: the wordlist or Biblical Terms? Why?

Next step: The next time you look at a wordlist or Biblical Terms status with a team, ask how the approvals happened. Do not look only at what the status shows now.

Coming up: Lesson 3 covers parallel passages. Your job there is to confirm the check ran against the team's own agreed approach. Then you route what it finds back to the team. You do not judge the language yourself.

docs.title: Lesson 3: Parallel Passages
docs.text:
Estimated time: 25 minutes

Purpose: Support a team through the parallel passages check. You confirm that every parallel passage has really been reviewed since the last revision. You point out patterns in the tool, and you leave every decision about wording to the team.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
You will be able to:

  • Confirm every parallel passage has actually been reviewed since the last revision, using the Parallel Passages tool's Status column.
  • Flag any verse pairings still showing a red "?" back to the team for their own decision.
  • Recognize signs of over-harmonising to raise with the team.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text: ✏️ Reflection: You usually do not speak the language a team is translating into. Think about a check like "do these two parallel passages say the same thing?" What can you judge yourself? What must stay the team's decision? Keep that line in mind through this lesson.

docs.title: Your role: process, not language
docs.text:
You cannot judge whether two passages in the team's language say the same thing. So your job here is process:

  • confirm the check was run;
  • confirm the team reviewed what it found;
  • hand every decision about wording back to the team.

docs.title: What the tool shows
docs.text:
The Parallel Passages tool opens in its own window. It shows passages that should say the same thing side by side. Examples are the Gospel accounts of the same event, or repeated Old Testament passages. It also shows the original-language text and gloss.

The tool shows where the passages match. It does not judge them. It does not flag "inconsistencies" the way a wordlist or Biblical Terms check does. The team looks at each pair and decides whether the translation is acceptable.

docs.title: Reading the shading
docs.text:
The tool shades matching text in every text it shows: the project's translation, the Greek and any resources.

  • Green: the same three or more words appear in both passages. The green may look paler in the translation and resources than in the Greek.
  • No shading: the text differs.
  • Yellow (in the Greek): a biblical scholar marked these words by hand as equivalent. This is usually a word with a different gloss. Yellow is not an exact match, but it is still a match. Count it as shaded.

This means you can compare the shading of the Greek with the shading of the translation. You do not need to read either one. Where the Greek is unshaded, the originals differ. So the translation may differ there too.

Two patterns are worth pointing out to the team:

  • The Greek is shaded, but the translation is not. The translation differs where the originals agree.
  • The translation is shaded, but the Greek is not. The translation may be more harmonized than the originals.

Do not expect the shading to line up word for word. The translation's word order can differ from the Greek. What matters is that the passages are similar where the originals are similar. The words do not need to come in the same order.

Compare the shading, not the words: Greek, translation and resource are shaded the same way.

NOTE: Either pattern is something to point out. It is not an error. Not every language can word things the same way. So some variation is acceptable, even where the originals agree. Whether the difference is right is the team's decision.

docs.title: The Status column
docs.text:
The tool tracks review status for each verse, in a Status column:

  • A checkmark means the verse pairing was reviewed and approved.
  • A red question mark (?) means the verse was edited after it was approved. It needs another look.

Use the dropdown above the table to show only the rows that need attention:

Checkmark = reviewed and approved; red "?" = edited since approval, needs another look.

On a flagged row, click the "Show differences" icon. It opens the two verses side by side, so you can see exactly what changed:

Show the team every verse that still has a red "?". Do not decide yourself whether the passages are consistent.

docs.title: Watch for over-harmonising
docs.text:
The common mistake here is over-harmonising. A team, or a checker who is too keen, makes parallel passages match more closely than the original texts do. Different biblical authors may tell a story differently. Parallel passages should be no more harmonized than the original texts.

That judgment belongs to the team. Where it becomes a content question about Scripture, it may belong to a Translation Consultant. Your role is to make sure each red "?" got a real decision. It must not be left unreviewed, or quietly over-corrected.

WARNING: A team may say "we already checked the parallel passages." They may be remembering an earlier pass, before later revisions changed those verses. Editing a verse after approval turns its checkmark back into a red "?". So open the tool yourself and look at the Status column. This is the same "we already did that" trap from Lesson 1.

Key takeaways

  • Your job is process and routing. Decisions about wording belong to the team.
  • The tool shows matches but does not judge them. Compare the shading of the Greek with the shading of the translation. Yellow counts as shaded.
  • Checkmark = reviewed and approved. Red "?" = edited since approval, needs another look.
  • Parallel passages should be no more harmonized than the original texts.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
✏️ Try this: Three exercises on this lesson. Try each one without looking back. Then check your answers against the Content section above.

  1. Sort the shading. For each situation, write what it may mean. Then write whether it is one of the two patterns to point out to the team.
  2. (a) The Greek is shaded green, and the translation is shaded.
  3. (b) The Greek is shaded, but the translation is unshaded.
  4. (c) The Greek is unshaded, but the translation is shaded.
  5. (d) The Greek is shaded yellow, and the translation is shaded.
  6. (e) The Greek is unshaded, and the translation is unshaded.
  7. Explain why it is not your decision. Write the standard parallel passages are held to, in one sentence. Name the mistake that comes from missing it. Then explain why the team judges the translation against that standard, and not you. You can spot the shading patterns yourself, so say why that is not enough.
  8. Apply the Status column. A team says they checked parallel passages two months ago. Since then they have done a revision pass. Write:
  9. what you open, and what you look for;
  10. what you do with each verse that shows a red "?";
  11. what must be true before a difference counts as decided.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Think of a team you support where you do not speak the project language. Have you ever started to judge content instead of confirming process? How could you word your feedback so the line stays clear?

Next step: Before your next check-review session, write one sentence you can use to hand a content decision back to the team. It should not sound like you are avoiding the work. For example: "That's a decision for your team. My job is to make sure the check ran and you've seen everything it found."

Coming up: Lesson 4 covers numbers and measures. You confirm which numbers and measures list the team's Paratext version has, and you leave the renderings to the team.

docs.title: Lesson 4: Numbers and Measures
docs.text:
Estimated time: 20 minutes

Purpose: Support a team through checking numbers, weights and measures. You confirm which Biblical Terms list the team's Paratext version actually has for them. The team reviews the renderings in it against their own agreed approach. You leave every decision about renderings to the team.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
You will be able to:

  • Confirm which numbers/measures list is actually available for the team's Paratext version — the new combined list, or only the older Numbers list with no Measures list.
  • Coach the team to review the renderings in whichever list is available against their already-agreed approach.
  • Route any gaps or contradictions back to the team rather than deciding the correct rendering yourself.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text: ✏️ Reflection: In Lesson 3 you left decisions about wording to the team. Numbers and measures work the same way. Think of a team you support. Do you know which Paratext version they use? Do you know where their decisions about money, weights and measures are written down? Keep those two questions in mind through this lesson.

docs.title: Your role: process, not language
docs.text: You do not decide whether a number or a measure is rendered correctly. As with parallel passages, your job is process. You confirm which list is available, make sure the team reviews it, and route what they find back to the team.

docs.title: The lists are changing
docs.text:
Numbers and measures are not checked in Basic Checks. They are reviewed in Biblical Terms lists, and these lists are changing:

  • A new, combined list covers numbers, weights and measures together, in one list. It is expected to become available before too long.
  • It replaces the older, separate Numbers list.
  • There is no Measures list. Measures was never released as its own list. Its terms are being folded into the new combined list.
  • The new version does not reach every team at the same time. Some teams will stay on an older, unmigrated version for a while.

So always confirm what the team's Paratext version actually has before you rely on it.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
Numbers appears as a separate entry in Paratext's Open Biblical Terms List dialog. Once it is available, the new combined list appears there as its own entry too. Other, unrelated lists sit alongside them, such as Major Biblical Terms, All Biblical Terms, NT Key Biblical Terms, Inclusive/Exclusive Pronouns and Younger/Older Siblings.

You saw this dialog in Lesson 2. Check what is actually listed in this team's project.

Do not assume a project's lists match what you have seen elsewhere.

docs.title: The two situations you may find
docs.text:
1. The new combined list is available. Confirm it is there. Then the team reviews its renderings against their documented approach to numbers, weights and measures.
  2. Only the older, separate Numbers list is available. There is no Measures list. Numbers has fairly limited scope. Confirm the team actually reviewed it, and did not assume it was clean from an earlier pass. Numbers does not cover weights and measures. So coach the team to add the measurement terms they need to their project Biblical Terms list:
  3. In Major Biblical Terms, open the Biblical Terms Filter and choose the Realia category. Many measurement terms are there.
  4. All Biblical Terms has more, but no categories. The team searches for the ones they need.

This is tedious, which is why the new list is being built. Then the team reviews those renderings against their documented approach.

WARNING: Do not compare the measure renderings yourself. It is possible to do some of this by hand, but it is not easy. Ambiguous terms will slip past you. Anything inconsistent the team finds stays with them to resolve.

docs.title: Check against the team's agreed approach
docs.text:
Most teams decide early how to handle numbers, weights, money and measures for the whole project. For example, they decide whether to convert ancient measures to modern ones, or how to render currency. They do not decide case by case.

  • The team reviews the renderings in whichever list is available against this already-agreed, documented approach.
  • The team's review may find a gap or a contradiction. For example, a rendering does not match the approach, or two occurrences of the same measure do not match. Refer it back to the team to resolve. Do not decide the correct rendering yourself.
  • The team may have no documented approach for a kind of measurement. Then that comes first. The team agrees and documents its approach before anyone resolves single inconsistencies. You cannot judge an inconsistency without a standard to check it against.

NOTE: There is no confirmed field case yet of a specific numbers, weights or measures error caught by either list. So this lesson does not give one. Stay alert, and do not assume a known pattern.

Key takeaways

  • Numbers and the new combined list are separate entries. There is no Measures list.
  • Confirm what this team's Paratext version actually has before you rely on it.
  • The team reviews the renderings against its documented approach. Route any gap back to the team.
  • Where there is no combined list, the team adds the measurement terms to its project Biblical Terms list and reviews the renderings. You do not compare them yourself.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
✏️ Try this: Three exercises on this lesson. Try each one without looking back. Then check your answers against the Content section above.

  1. Two situations that look alike.
  2. (a) The team's review finds that two occurrences of the same measurement do not match.
  3. (b) There is no documented, agreed approach for that kind of measurement at all.

Write one line for each situation, naming your next action. Then write one line on which one you must settle first when both are true, and why. 2. Which list does this team actually have? Open the Open Biblical Terms List dialog in a project you support. Note what is actually listed. Then write: - which of the two situations this team is in; - one line on what you would tell the team the list does and does not cover. 3. One question, one sentence. Write the question you would ask a team to find out where their agreed approach to numbers, weights, money and measures is written down. It could be a project note on a single term. More likely, because there are many terms, it is one reference document. Aim your question at finding whichever one exists. If your sentence hints at what the rendering should be, rewrite it.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Think again about the team from the Connect section. If they are on an older Paratext version, how would you explain that their version has no list for weights and measures? How would you coach them to add the measurement terms to their project list and review them, without doing it for them?

Next step: Before your next support session with that team, ask the question you wrote in Challenge 3. Note which Paratext version they use and which numbers and measures list it has.

Coming up: Lesson 5 turns to formatting checks and references. You work structural-first through chapter and verse numbers, marker pairs, headings and references. Lesson 6 then covers the Punctuation Inventory ahead of typesetting.

docs.title: Lesson 5: Structural Checks
docs.text:
Estimated time: 45 minutes

Purpose: Support a team through the structural formatting checks: chapter and verse numbers, marker pairs, headings, book titles, references and footnotes. You work in a fixed order, so that one early error does not hide behind many later ones. You coach the team to a real zero-error result, not just a fast one.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
You will be able to:

  • Diagnose formatting-check failures by working structural-first: chapter and verse numbering errors, unclosed marker pairs, ghost markers, wrong markers, and errors in book titles, section headings and references.
  • Coach a team to a zero-error result without touching their keyboard.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text: ✏️ Reflection: Think about the last time you opened a project's Basic Checks and saw a long list of formatting errors. Where did you start? Did you fix the first error in the list? Or did you look for a pattern that might cause several errors at once? Keep that in mind. This lesson is about finding the structural cause before you chase single errors.

docs.title: One missing marker, many errors
docs.text:
Formatting errors can spread. One error in the structure can cause many others further down. Here is a common, real example.

A section heading (\s1) must be followed by a paragraph marker such as \p. If the \p is missing, Paratext treats everything after the heading text as part of the heading. This continues until the next paragraph-style marker (\p, \m, \q and so on). Verse numbers and verse text are swallowed into the heading style.

You may see:

  • a heading that is much too big or looks wrong, because the verses are now part of it;
  • verse numbers that seem to have disappeared from the normal text;
  • references that count wrongly, because the check reads the swallowed verses as part of the heading.

In Run Basic Checks, this has a clear signature. You see two errors for every swallowed verse:

  • "Verse number in heading"
  • "Marker cannot occur here: \v"

One missing paragraph marker, and the verse numbers disappear into the heading.

If you start with the errors at the bottom of a long list, you may fix symptoms of one cause higher up. So work in the order below.

docs.title: The structural-first order: steps 1–4
docs.text:
1. Chapter/Verse Numbers. Run this check in Run Basic Checks first. It sits alongside Markers, Characters, Punctuation, References and Footnote quotes. Every other check reports its results by chapter and verse. If the numbering has errors (such as a duplicate verse), you cannot trust those locations.

Confirm this one first — everything else on this list depends on it.

  1. Marker-pair census. Paratext has two kinds of markers:
  2. Paragraph markers (\p, \s, \q and so on) stand alone and apply to a whole paragraph.
  3. Paired markers (\f...\f*, \x...\x*, character styles and so on) wrap a piece of text. They must open and close correctly.

Open the Markers Inventory (Tools > Checking Inventories > Markers Inventory). Check that every paired marker closes. One unclosed pair is often the single cause of a whole group of errors.

This is where you check that every paired marker actually closes.

  1. Ghost markers. Look for markers with no content. They are often left behind when someone deletes a footnote or cross-reference but not its marker. You may see nothing wrong on screen, but they can break export and typesetting.
  2. Long/short verses. Compare verse length with the source. A verse that is much longer or shorter can mean a misplaced verse marker, two verses merged, or missing text. Rule this out before you treat other errors in the chapter as heading or reference problems.

docs.title: The structural-first order: steps 5–8
docs.text:
1. Section headings. The marker itself is rarely wrong. Most projects use \s1 almost always, and \s2 only sometimes. You check structure, not wording:
  2. Each heading is present, uses a heading marker, and has not swallowed verse text.
  3. Compare where the headings fall with the LWC (Language of Wider Communication) Bible. The LWC Bible is your main cross-check. It shows where a heading might be missing or misplaced, without you reading the language.
  4. A heading in a different place is a question for the team, not an error. Their language may divide the passage differently from the LWC.
  5. Whether the wording fits the passage is the team's decision. Pass that question to them.

NOTE: A back translation helps only if someone made it by hand, outside Paratext. A back translation made in Paratext carries the translation's own headings, so comparing against it proves nothing.

  1. Book titles. This is a consistency check. Book titles should follow a similar style across the whole Bible. In English, the problem would look like this:
  2. one book is "The Gospel of Mark", another is just "Matthew", and a third is "The Gospel written by Luke";
  3. books in a series don't follow one pattern. Books such as 1 and 2 Corinthians, or 1, 2 and 3 John, should be numbered and named the same way.

You can check this without knowing the language. Most book names are names of people or places, such as Mark, Corinth or John. You can usually recognise the name in each title, then compare the words around it. - Show the team where the style differs. - Let the team choose the style. 7. References and the table of contents. \r shows parallel passages. \xt is the cross-reference marker. Look for: - book names that were missed in checking; - \r abbreviations from another language. A common cause is copying many \r lines from another NT project as a starting point. They bring that project's abbreviations with them; - a table of contents that does not match the book titles in the text. 8. Footnotes. A footnote can pass the marker check in step 2 and still be on the wrong verse, or appear twice. Deciding which verse a footnote belongs to needs someone who reads the text. So this review belongs to the team: - Ask the team to check footnote placement book by book. - Look for \fq markers in the Markers Inventory. A \fq marks text from the verse that is quoted inside a footnote. If the project has any, the team must run the Footnote quotes check in Run Basic Checks. Any edit to the verse can leave the quote out of date.

NOTE: An unclosed \f (a footnote opened without its \f*) does much less harm than a missing \p. If it is unclosed at the end of a verse, it has no effect. If it is unclosed partway through a verse, the footnote text shows as part of the verse. That is all. It does not spread into headings, references or other markers.

Working structural-first does not mean the team must fix errors in this exact order. It means you look for the biggest single cause first. Then you do not send the team to correct fifty symptoms of one unclosed marker.

docs.title: Denied errors: a result can look clean when it is not
docs.text:
In Paratext you can deny a flagged error. This is meant for errors that are not really errors. In one field case, a team denied errors they did not understand. They cleared the flags instead of fixing the problems. (In the wordlist, the same shortcut is marking every word Correct — see Lesson 2.)

When a denied error is shown, it appears with strikethrough text. But whether it shows at all depends on View > Denied messages. With that option off, denied errors disappear from the list. The list shows only "Denied message(s) not shown."

Denied errors are struck through — but only if this view option is on.

With the view option off, the list simply tells you denied messages exist without showing them.

WARNING: Zero formatting errors does not always mean the project is clean. It can also mean: - the checks were run early and not run again after later changes; or - errors were denied and are hidden from view.

Confirm the team ran the checks again at this stage. Turn on View > Denied messages before you trust a zero-error result. This is the same "we already did that" trap from earlier lessons.

Key takeaways

  • Work structural-first. Check chapter and verse numbers first, then marker pairs and ghost markers, before headings, titles and references.
  • You diagnose the cause and coach the team to fix it. You never touch their keyboard.
  • Trust a zero-error result only if the checks were run again at this stage and View > Denied messages is on.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
✏️ Try this: Three exercises on this lesson. Try each one without looking back. Then check your answers against the Content section above. The aim is to find your gaps now, not in the middle of a support session.

  1. Put the steps in order. Here are the eight structural-first steps, mixed up: footnotes · ghost markers · book titles · chapter/verse numbers · references · long/short verses · marker pairs · section headings. Write them in the right order. Then, for the first three, write one line each on why that step comes before headings, titles and references.
  2. Two unclosed markers, two very different effects.
  3. For a missing \p after a \s1 heading: write what gets swallowed, and up to what point.
  4. For a \f opened without its \f*: write what happens if it is unclosed at the end of a verse, and what happens if it is unclosed partway through a verse.
  5. Then say which of the two spreads into other markers in the chapter, and which does not. This difference stops you treating a small error as a big one.
  6. A denied error is not a fixed one. Write one line each:
  7. how a denied error looks when it is visible;
  8. which View menu setting controls whether it shows at all;
  9. what the same shortcut is in the wordlist.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Think of a team you support. Which errors come up most often in their Basic Checks? Every language and project has its own. Could some of them come from one cause higher up, such as a missing marker? How would you explain to the team why you check chapter and verse numbers first, even when there are only a few of those errors?

Next step: Before your next formatting-check session, write down the structural-first order (chapter/verse numbers → marker pairs → ghost markers → long/short verses → headings → book titles → references → footnotes). Put it somewhere you will have it in front of you.

Coming up: Lesson 6 covers the Punctuation Inventory and Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation. These are the last checks to do before the project goes to a typesetter.

docs.title: Lesson 6: Punctuation Before Typesetting
docs.text:
Estimated time: 35 minutes

Purpose: Before a project goes to a typesetter, make sure the team has really reviewed Paratext's Punctuation Inventory and Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation. Problems found here are cheap to fix. The same problems found by the typesetter cost much more.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
You will be able to:

  • Review and use Paratext's Punctuation Inventory (Tools > Checking Inventories > Punctuation Inventory) before typesetting.
  • Select "Show sequences" in its Inventory menu, so that Run Basic Checks' punctuation checkbox changes to "Punctuation (sequences)" and checks multi-character punctuation sequences, not just a plain "Punctuation" check.
  • Use the Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation inventory (Tools > Checking Inventories) to find single unmatched bracket or parenthesis characters.
  • Confirm that both inventories were really reviewed, not just assumed to be done.
  • Recognize the settings problems that create extra work for a typesetter.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text: ✏️ Reflection: Think of a project you support that is close to typesetting. Who will see punctuation problems first: the team, you or the typesetter? If the typesetter finds them, who fixes them, and how long does it take? Keep that question in mind. This lesson is about finding those problems while they are still cheap to fix.

docs.title: Two Paratext tools for punctuation
docs.text:
Both tools are in Paratext, under Tools > Checking Inventories. Neither is part of PTXprint or anything the typesetter runs. Reviewing them is part of your own formatting check.

  • Punctuation Inventory lists every punctuation character used in the project. With "Show sequences" selected, it also covers multi-character sequences. For example, several quotation marks together, or a quotation mark next to a space or a ")".
  • Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation opens in its own window. It lists single unmatched bracket or parenthesis characters, such as "}", "[" or "(". Each row has a count and a Status column: a checkmark means approved, a red X means incorrect, and a blue "?" means it needs review.

The two tools work together. Each catches something the other does not, so one does not replace the other.

docs.title: Why this matters before typesetting
docs.text: One consultant spent a lot of time with a typesetter after the project was handed over. Together they sorted out the Punctuation Inventory's settings. The team could have fixed these problems earlier, during their own formatting review.

docs.title: What to do
docs.text:
1. Confirm someone really opened and reviewed both inventories at this stage. When a project is nearly finished, it is easy to assume they "must be fine by now".
  2. Check the Punctuation Inventory's settings, not just its list of characters. Unresolved characters in the settings come back later as a long list of problems for the typesetter.
  3. Select "Show sequences" in the Punctuation Inventory tab's Inventory menu.
  4. Run the punctuation check in Run Basic Checks.
  5. Review Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation directly, using its Status column.

NOTE: Whether a flagged character is valid is an orthography question. If you have the orthography statement written by the project's linguist, check the character against it. If not, the team decides.

docs.title: How "Show sequences" changes Run Basic Checks
docs.text:
The punctuation checkbox in Run Basic Checks just chooses which check to run. "Show sequences" changes what that check does:

  • With "Show sequences" selected, the checkbox is labelled "Punctuation (sequences)". It checks multi-character sequences.
  • Without it, the checkbox stays labelled "Punctuation". It checks only single characters.

This checkbox is what makes "Punctuation (sequences)" mean anything.

Each flagged result shows a combination Paratext does not recognize, with its reference. Many involve quotation marks next to other punctuation:

This is what a flagged sequence actually looks like.

NOTE: This lesson covers punctuation sequences only. Quotation marks themselves are more complex. Paratext checks them with a separate Quotation check, covered in the Paratext Quotation Rules course, starting with Lesson 1, "What the Quotation Check Does."

"Show sequences" does not cover single unmatched brackets. That is the job of Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation:

A direct list of unmatched brackets and parentheses. It shows only the characters that are actually unmatched in the project.

WARNING: "We're nearly done" does not mean "someone reviewed the punctuation." Before the project reaches a typesetter, confirm that both inventories were actually opened and reviewed at this stage.

Key takeaways

  • Both inventories are in Paratext (Tools > Checking Inventories). Review them yourself; don't leave them to the typesetter.
  • Confirm both were really reviewed at this stage, not assumed clean.
  • Unresolved Punctuation Inventory settings become extra work for the typesetter later.
  • Select "Show sequences" so the check becomes "Punctuation (sequences)". Without it, sequences are not checked. (Quotation marks have their own Quotation check.)
  • Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation and "Show sequences" each catch different problems. Use both.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
✏️ Try this: Three exercises on this lesson. Try each one without looking back. Then check your answers against the Content section above.

  1. Check one setting. In a project you already support, open Tools > Checking Inventories > Punctuation Inventory. Open its Inventory menu and see whether "Show sequences" is selected. Write down what you found. Then write one sentence: how is the Run Basic Checks punctuation checkbox labelled, and what does it check, when the option is off? And when it is on? This is one setting, not a full review.
  2. A review can be real and still incomplete. Imagine a consultant carefully reviews the Punctuation Inventory, but "Show sequences" is not selected. In two lines, say what their review missed, and what would have made it complete. Then name the difference between a false-clean result caused by a skipped step and one caused by an unselected setting.
  3. Two tools, one gap each. In the same project, open Tools > Checking Inventories > Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation. Write one line on what it lists that "Show sequences" does not. Write one line on what "Show sequences" catches that Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation does not.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Think again of your project that is close to typesetting. Has anyone, team or you, opened the Punctuation Inventory and Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation recently? Or is everyone assuming they are clean? What would it cost to check now, compared with hearing about it later from a frustrated typesetter?

Next step: Add this standing question for every project close to typesetting: "Punctuation Inventory and Unmatched Pairs of Punctuation — both really reviewed?"

Coming up: Lessons 7 and 8 turn to glossary linking and the final layout and draft-PDF read-through. As with the Punctuation Inventory here, you will do hands-on technical setup alongside your coaching role.

docs.title: Lesson 7: Glossary Linking
docs.text:
Estimated time: 30 minutes

Purpose: Support a team through the glossary-linking operation. You check that each glossary term is linked at the right scope: the first time it appears in each section, not every time. If the scope is wrong, you coach the team to fix it.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
You will be able to:

  • Diagnose over-linked glossary marking (every occurrence instead of first-per-section).
  • Coach a team to unlink and relink at the correct scope.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text: ✏️ Reflection: Think of a printed book with a glossary at the back. A small mark in the text tells you that a word is in the glossary. How useful is that mark the first time you meet a hard word? How useful is it the tenth time, on the same page? This lesson is about putting a glossary link where the reader needs it, and nowhere else.

docs.title: Content
docs.text: NOTE: This course covers the glossary-linking operation and its checks — the marks in the text. Glossary content (what goes in the glossary, and writing the entries) is out of scope; a separate course will cover it. This lesson assumes the team already has a glossary.

docs.title: Over-linking: the common mistake
docs.text:
A glossary link belongs at the first occurrence of a term in each section. That is the first place a reader is likely to need the definition.

The common field mistake is over-linking: the team links every occurrence of the term. The reader sees the same glossary mark again and again, and the link loses its purpose. In one field case, the consultant unlinked the terms. Then the consultant relinked them at "first occurrence in every section," not "all occurrences."

docs.title: Check with Find, not the link report
docs.text:
The glossary-link operation gives no pass/fail result. Its report of linked occurrences is transient. It is replaced as soon as you link the next item or group. Teams often link in batches, because the operation is complicated, so earlier reports are gone. The row count does not help either: some terms are simply more frequent than others.

So use Paratext's Find. You can run it again at any time. Search the project for the glossary term (for example, "angel").

Glossary links are marked with \w and \w* around the linked words, in the form \w <surface text>|<rendering>\w*. For example:

  • \w angel messenja guy\w*
  • \w angel guy|Angel messenja guy\w* — used when the words in the text differ from the glossary entry's own rendering.

This is the markup a correctly-scoped link leaves behind.

You can also see this markup in the text editor. The rendering half of a \w...\w* marker shows in light grey in the running text, so you can scan a passage by eye.

The grey text is the marker's rendering half — visible right in the text, not just in Find results.

Look at each Find result:

  • Markup around every occurrence of the term means over-linking.
  • Markup around only the first occurrence in each section means the scope is correct.

To fix over-linking, unlink the extra links. Then relink at "first occurrence in every section." You can do this in the tool yourself, because links are markup, not translated text. You still never change the team's translation itself.

WARNING: Do not trust the number of Find results. Find also matches the same words inside the rendering half of an existing \w...\w* marker. Open each result. Check whether it has its own markup, or sits inside another marker's rendering.

docs.title: A term inside a longer term
docs.text:
Glossary terms can overlap. For example, "Holy Spirit" is a phrase term, and "Spirit" is also a term on its own. If you search for "Spirit", a result may sit inside a marker whose rendering is "Holy Spirit". That is correct. The word is linked to the phrase term, and it should not also be linked as "Spirit".

This is why phrase terms are linked before the single words inside them. So when a result sits inside a marker, read the rendering before you flag it.

TIP: To check every linked term at once, type regex: in Find (no space after the colon), then search for \w[^\]*\w\*. This returns every \w...\w* occurrence in one search. (A test search found 22 in Matthew alone.)

docs.title: Watch for a false-clean result here too
docs.text:
The Project Plan task "Check and link glossary entries" (Stage 6, Final Preparation for Publication) has its own checkbox. A person ticks it; Paratext does not set it from the linking data. As with any Project Plan status (Lesson 1), treat it as a starting point, not proof. A Find search of the markup shows whether the scope is right.

Key takeaways

  • Link at the first occurrence in every section. To fix over-linking, unlink, then relink at that scope. You can do this yourself.
  • The link report disappears, so check with Find. Read the markup on each result; do not trust the count.
  • A result inside a longer phrase term's marker is correct.
  • A ticked Project Plan checkbox does not prove the linking was reviewed.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
✏️ Try this: Three exercises on this lesson. Try each one without looking back. Then check your answers against the Content section above.

  1. Choose your check. Write one line on why the linked-occurrences report is not a reliable check once linking is done. Then name the tool you would use instead.
  2. Sort the Find results. You search a project for "Spirit". For each result below, write over-linked, correct, or count proves nothing:
  3. a. In one section, only the first occurrence is wrapped in a \w...\w* marker. The other occurrences in that section are plain text.
  4. b. In one section, every occurrence is wrapped in its own \w...\w* marker.
  5. c. The word sits inside a marker whose rendering is "Holy Spirit".
  6. d. Find shows 40 results for the term in one book.
  7. Name the fix. Write the two steps that fix over-linking. Use the tool's own wording for the correct scope. Then say in one line why that scope helps the reader.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Think of a team you support that will soon link its glossary. Will they link in batches? How will you check their work after the link report is gone? What would you say if the team shows you a ticked Project Plan checkbox?

Next step: Before your next glossary-linking session, try the regex: search from this lesson in a project you can open. Then you will know what the results look like before you sit down with a team.

Coming up: Lesson 8 covers layout and hyphenation decisions for print, and the final PTXprint draft-PDF read-through.

docs.title: Lesson 8: Layout and the Draft-PDF Read-Through
docs.text:
Estimated time: 35 minutes

Purpose: Support a team through layout and hyphenation decisions for print. Then lead the final PTXprint draft-PDF read-through. These are the last checks before the team's files go to the typesetter.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
You will be able to:

  • Advise a team on a single- versus two-column layout, based on what readers and the community expect, not just word length.
  • Use the Wordlist's Show hyphenation view to draft, enter and approve hyphenation breaks, one at a time and in batches.
  • Make sure the team confirms each break, so long words break correctly in a two-column layout.

You will be able to:

  • Lead a team through the final PTXprint draft-PDF read-through.
  • Resolve or triage what it finds, and leave true typesetting composition to the typesetter.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text: ✏️ Reflection: Picture the very last read-through before a team's files go to the typesetter. Small things are easy to miss here: a word alone at the top of a column, a footnote that moved to another page, a heading in an awkward place. This is the last chance to catch them. How sharp is your attention at the end of a long review? This lesson helps you build habits that work on any day.

docs.title: Layout: start with what readers expect
docs.text:
In one field case, an expat project admin chose a single-column layout. The language has long words, and the team had never used hyphenation.

But the community does not yet have a Bible in its own language. It reads Bibles in a Language of Wider Communication (LWC), a regional trade language. Those LWC Bibles are printed in two columns, so readers expect two columns. That expectation is the baseline, even if the LWC does not have the long-word problem. The layout had to be two-column. Long words only told the team that it needed hyphenation.

Your role has two parts:

  1. Advise. Ask what layout the community's LWC Bibles and other printed materials use. Do not choose a layout just because it avoids a technical problem.
  2. Do the technical setup. Once two columns is the right choice, set up hyphenation in the Wordlist.

docs.title: Show hyphenation in the Wordlist
docs.text:
1. Add the hyphen to the word-medial punctuation list: Project > Project settings > Language settings > Other Characters tab. Most Roman-script languages use the hyphen to break words. Other scripts may use a different character.
  2. Open Tools > Wordlist.
  3. From the Wordlist's own tab menu, choose View > Show hyphenation. It sits next to "Show morphology" and "Show spelling status".
  4. A hyphenation column appears. It shows Paratext's guessed break points for each word.
  5. Equal signs mark the breaks, for example an=ti=no=mi=an=ism. Each = is a place where the word may break across a column.

Each word also has a tick:

  • A grey tick means Paratext guessed the breaks. No one has reviewed them yet.
  • A green tick means the breaks are approved.

Grey = Paratext's guess; green = a human confirmed it.

docs.title: The team decides each break
docs.text:
Where a word may break is a fact about the language. You do not speak the language. So neither Paratext's guess nor your own impression settles it. The team decides each break. You do the drafting and the tool work.

  1. Ask the team for their orthography statement.
  2. If they have one, draft breaks from the syllable structure it describes. Add or remove = marks on Paratext's guesses where its syllable rules point.
  3. An orthography statement is not always final. Translation can start with a trial orthography, and the community may not accept every choice in it. Ask whether the statement is still current, and whether the community has accepted it.
  4. If the team cannot find it, it does not describe syllable structure, or it is still a trial orthography, do not guess. The team proposes the breaks, and you enter them in the Wordlist.
  5. Have the team review and confirm each break. Go through the drafted and guessed breaks with a team member who speaks the language and also writes it well. Not every speaker reads well or spells consistently, and the New Testament may be the largest book ever printed in the language. They say whether each break is right. Where the team is unsure, they check with community members who read and write the language well. Readers notice a word broken in the wrong place.
  6. If they say a break is wrong, click the word. Add or remove = marks where they say the breaks fall. The tick turns green automatically when you edit the word.
  7. Approve one confirmed word: click its grey tick.
  8. The tick turns green. The word is approved.
  9. Approve a group of confirmed words: select the first word. Shift-click to select a run of words, or Ctrl-click to pick separate words. Then use the Wordlist's tab menu > Edit > Approve word hyphenation.
  10. Every selected word is approved at once.
  11. Before the files go to print, check that no grey ticks remain on words the team has not reviewed.

WARNING: When you edit a word, its tick turns green before the team has seen it. So the breaks you drafted look approved already. Keep a note of the words you drafted. Then the team's review covers those words as well as the grey ticks.

TIP: As more words are approved, Paratext's guesses get better. Late in the review, the team may confirm a run of words at a glance, and batch approval saves the most time. The team still confirms each break; batch approval only records it faster.

The approvals save to hyphenatedWords.txt in the project folder when you close the Wordlist. A line with a leading * is team-approved. A line without * is still an unapproved Paratext guess.

WARNING: PTXprint's draft-PDF export uses unapproved guesses as well as approved hyphenation, so a draft can look fine with guesses unreviewed. Approve hyphenation before the files go to print.

NOTE: Two things to watch for: - In a Study Bible Publication project, the Wordlist is view-only. You cannot approve hyphenation there. - Word break characters are not only for non-Roman scripts. The hyphen you added to the word-medial punctuation list is one. Hyphenation adds hyphens as word break characters, but only uses them when a word falls near a line end.

TIP: For unusual cases, hyphenatedWords.txt can be edited by hand to customize hard/soft hyphens and hyphenated markers (HardHyphen, SoftHyphen, SoftHyphenOut, HyphenatedMarkers). Most teams do not need this.

docs.title: The final PTXprint draft-PDF read-through
docs.text:
This is the team's last look before the typesetter. Work through the full draft PDF in PTXprint, and watch for five things:

  • Spreads — how facing pages look together, not just one by one. Check that each pair looks balanced.
  • Orphan words — a single word left alone at the top or bottom of a column or page.
  • Footnote shifts — a footnote that has moved to a different page from its reference.
  • Heading placement — a heading in an awkward place at a page or column break.
  • Underfilled pages — a page with much more white space than the pages next to it.

A heading held together with its paragraph pushed the whole block to the next column — leaving this underfilled gap behind it.

The read-through also finds composition issues outside this list. Examples are picture size and spacing, and page-margin spacing.

An oversized picture, and one crowded too close to its own credit text — both are typesetting-craft issues to flag, not fix yourself.

Not enough top-margin space between the running header and the body text below it.

NOTE: This course's team workbook material was checked against PTXprint 3.0.38. PTXprint updates often, so menu labels may have moved. Check against the version in front of you. Underfilled-page auto-fill is available from PTXprint v3.0.19+. On an older installation, check that the feature exists before you rely on it.

docs.title: Resolve what you can, triage the rest
docs.text:
For each issue the read-through finds, decide whose it is:

  • Yours to fix — for example, a linking or markup scope issue.
  • The team's call — anything about the content.
  • The typesetter's — true typesetting composition. This is the typesetter's craft. Do not try to solve it yourself.

Key takeaways

  • Layout follows what readers expect, such as two-column LWC Bibles, not word length alone.
  • In the Wordlist, you draft or enter the breaks and approve them (grey tick to green), one at a time or in batches. The team decides whether each break is right.
  • Approve all hyphenation before print. PTXprint's draft PDF uses unapproved guesses too.
  • In the read-through, watch for spreads, orphan words, footnote shifts, heading placement and underfilled pages. Then triage each issue: yours, the team's, or the typesetter's.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
✏️ Try this: Five short exercises on this lesson. Try each one without looking back. Then check your answers against the Content section above.

  1. Two criteria, one decision.
  2. Write one line on what long words can tell you about a layout choice.
  3. Write one line on what sets the baseline for the layout.
  4. Write one question you would ask the team about what the community already reads.
  5. Put the hyphenation steps in order. The team has an orthography statement. Here are the steps, mixed up: the team reviews and confirms each break · choose View > Show hyphenation · check that no unreviewed grey ticks remain · add the hyphen to word-medial punctuation in Language settings · open Tools > Wordlist · draft breaks from the orthography statement · approve confirmed words with Edit > Approve word hyphenation. Write them in order. Then answer in one line each:
  6. What changes if the orthography statement cannot be found, or does not describe syllable structure?
  7. A word you drafted already has a green tick. Why does it still need the team's review?
  8. Which read-through check is it? The read-through has five things to watch for: spreads, orphan words, footnote shifts, heading placement and underfilled pages. Each line below describes a problem on a draft page. Name which of the five it is:
  9. a. One word sits alone at the top of the second column.
  10. b. The footnote for a verse is printed on the next page, not on the verse's page.
  11. c. One page has much more white space at the bottom than the pages around it.
  12. d. A section heading sits at the very bottom of a column. Its paragraph starts in the next column.
  13. e. Each page looks fine alone. But side by side, the text on the left page ends several lines higher than the text on the right page, so the pair looks unbalanced.
  14. Yours, the team's, or the typesetter's? Write who should deal with each issue:
  15. a. A glossary term is linked at every occurrence in a section.
  16. b. A team member asks whether a heading's wording fits its passage.
  17. c. A picture is too big for the page.

Then write, in one line, the general test you used. 5. Check your own PTXprint. Find which PTXprint version is installed on the machine you would use with a team. Is it new enough for underfilled-page auto-fill? If it is not, update to the latest version.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: Think of a team you support. What layout do the LWC Bibles in their community use? Has anyone asked the team? Which of the five read-through checks are you most likely to miss when you are tired?

Next step: Before your next final read-through with a team, write down the five things to watch for: spreads, orphan words, footnote shifts, heading placement and underfilled pages. Put the list where you will have it open during the review.

Coming up: With the check areas covered, the scenario bank puts everything from this course together in mentor-reviewed, applied scenarios. These include the false-clean thread that runs through two of the core cases.

docs.title: Scenario bank
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60 minutes

Purpose: Seven scenarios that use the whole course. A mentor reviews your answers. These scenarios earn this course's 3 - Independent level (see 00-design.md, "Outcome-level open question").

  • Each core objective (2, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10) has its own scenario.
  • Scenario 7 combines the secondary objectives (3, 4, 8).
  • The false-clean thread (objective 1) runs inside Scenarios 1 and 3.

Every scenario comes from a confirmed SME field case, a known mistake pattern, or Lessons 1 to 8.

docs.title: For learners
docs.text:
1. Read each scenario carefully, including the context.
  2. For each scenario, write three things:
  3. how you would diagnose the situation;
  4. what you would say to the team;
  5. what you would escalate, if anything, and to whom.
  6. Send your written answers to your mentor.

docs.title: For mentors
docs.text:
• Use 10-mentor-guide.md. It says what to watch for in each answer. It also gives the "what good looks like" markers from the SME interview.
  • Score reasoning and coaching, not whether the learner names one "correct" fix. Several scenarios have more than one good answer.

docs.title: Scenario 1: The Harmonized Synoptics (Objective 2 — parallel passages)
docs.text:
Situation: A team is nearly at Stage 6. Two accounts of the same event have several differences in wording. The team lead says: "Those are supposed to be different. We're not changing them. We checked this months ago."

Context: You open the Parallel Passages tool and look at the verses side by side. Several verses show a red question mark in the Status column, not a checkmark. This means someone edited those verses in a revision some time ago, and nobody has reviewed them since. You don't speak the team's language, so you can't judge the meaning. But you can see the tool's shading on the Greek and on the team's translation.

NOTE: A reminder of how the shading works (Lesson 3): - Green shading marks the same three or more words in both passages. - In the Greek, yellow marks words a scholar has marked as equivalent. Yellow counts as shaded. - The shading may look paler in the translation and resources than in the Greek. - Word order can differ, so the shading need not line up word for word. - Unshaded Greek means the originals differ there.

A mismatch in shading is a question for the team, not an error. The team decides.

Your task:

  1. Diagnose.
  2. What would you confirm before you accept the team lead's explanation?
  3. How would you use the Status column to check whether these verses were reviewed after the last revision?
  4. How does what you find connect to the "we already did that" trap from Lesson 1?
  5. What could you learn by comparing the shading in the Greek with the shading in the translation?
  6. Say to the team. How would you ask the team to open the Parallel Passages tool and go through each verse that still has a red "?"? Say it without suggesting that you doubt their judgment about real variation.
  7. Escalate. The team's review may show that team members disagree. Some may think a difference is real variation; others may think it is an error. Who handles that: you, the team, or someone else? Say why.

docs.title: Scenario 2: The Undocumented Measure (Objective 5 — Numbers and Measures)
docs.text:
Situation: A team asks you to check their Bible for consistent numbers, weights and measures. Here is what happened:

  1. Their Paratext version does not have the new combined list for numbers, weights and measures. It has only the older, separate Numbers list. There is no Measures list. You confirm this, and the team reviews the Numbers list.
  2. You tell the team their version has no list for weights and measures. You coach them to add the measurement terms they need to their project Biblical Terms list, and to review those renderings.
  3. Their review finds two passages that render the same measurement in different ways.
  4. You ask about their documented approach to measures. They aren't sure one exists. Someone remembers "a decision early on", but nobody knows where it is written.

Context: The new combined list is expected soon, but it does not reach every Paratext version at once. This check area has no well-known field mistake, unlike the wordlist or Biblical Terms. Your job is to confirm which lists this team's version really has. The rest is process and routing, not finding a known error.

Your task:

  1. Diagnose.
  2. How would you confirm which lists this team's Paratext version has: the new combined list, or only the older Numbers list with no Measures list?
  3. Their version has no list for weights and measures. Why does the team, not you, add the measurement terms and review the renderings?
  4. What would you settle first: the inconsistency itself, or whether an agreed approach exists at all?
  5. What is the difference between "an inconsistency was found" and "the team has no documented standard to check against"?
  6. Say to the team.
  7. How would you explain what their Paratext version has and does not have yet?
  8. How would you help them find their earlier decision, or agree on one now? Do this without suggesting a rendering yourself.
  9. Escalate. Once the approach is written down, who decides which of the two renderings is correct? Could any version of this situation need a Translation Consultant, rather than staying within the team?

docs.title: Scenario 3: The Inventory Nobody Opened (Objective 6 — formatting checks)
docs.text:
Situation: A team's Basic Checks show a short list of formatting errors. They are all in the second half of Mark:

  • Several verses in a row, just after one section heading, each have a pair of errors: "Verse number in heading" and "Marker cannot occur here: \v".
  • There is also a reference that looks garbled.

In that passage, the verses after the heading appear in the heading's bold style. Their verse numbers are missing from the normal text. The team has not mentioned Chapter/Verse Numbers. They went straight to the marker and reference errors.

The team also says the Punctuation Inventory "was already checked when we started the project." Since then, the project has had two more revisions. It goes to a typesetter in three weeks.

Context: Time is short. The team wants to hand off soon and thinks both things are already done.

Your task:

  1. Diagnose.
  2. Before you work through the Basic Checks list from top to bottom, what would you check first, and why?
  3. Chapter/Verse Numbers has not been confirmed clean. Why must you confirm it before anything else, including the marker-pair census?
  4. Suppose you then find a missing \p marker after a section heading in Mark. What would that explain about the other errors, with the verse text swallowed into the heading style? How would you confirm it before you tell the team?
  5. What is wrong with treating "checked when we started the project" as up to date for the Punctuation Inventory?
  6. Say to the team.
  7. What would you say to get them to run Basic Checks again, structural-first?
  8. For the Punctuation Inventory, what exactly would you ask them to open and show you?
  9. Escalate.
  10. The Punctuation Inventory's settings may be really confusing. Or a character you don't recognise may only be a font display problem. Who do you bring in?
  11. If the question is whether a character is valid in the language at all, where does the answer come from?

docs.title: Scenario 4: The Every-Occurrence Glossary (Objective 7 — glossary linking)
docs.text:
Situation: You are reviewing a project's glossary links before the final read-through. The team linked the glossary in batches. Each batch's linked-occurrences report was replaced when the next batch ran, so no report is left. You want to check whether "angel", a frequent term in this book, was linked at the correct scope.

Context: The glossary already exists. Its content is not your job; you are only reviewing the linking.

Your task:

  1. Diagnose.
  2. There is no report. How would you use Find to check the scope of the "angel" links?
  3. What exactly would you look for in the markup of each Find result? How does it show the difference between over-linking (every occurrence) and correct linking (the first occurrence in each section)?
  4. How could Find's list of results mislead you if you only looked at it quickly?
  5. The glossary also has a phrase term that contains the word "angel", such as "angel of the Lord". A Find result for "angel" may fall inside a marker for that phrase. Is that something to fix, or is it correct? Explain why.
  6. Say to the team.
  7. Describe exactly how you would unlink the term and link it again at the correct scope.
  8. What would you tell the team about why "first occurrence in each section" matters for readers?
